title: Unit 5 Quiz · Model Deployment & Applications
instructions: 30 questions, 32 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: Which method can measure feature importance for ANY model by shuffling one column and measuring the drop in score?
questions.explain: Shuffling breaks the link between that feature and the target; the bigger the score drop, the more the model relied on it.

questions.q: The credit-score coefficient is −0.01455 per point. The odds ratio for +50 points, e^(−0.01455 × 50), is about:
For a logistic model, a feature’s contribution to one applicant’s log-odds (vs an average applicant) is:
questions.explain: Summing these contributions with the average log-odds gives the applicant’s exact log-odds; the biggest positive ones are the reason codes.

questions.q: “With a credit score of about 716, everything else unchanged, the loan would be approved.” This is a:
questions.explain: It states the smallest change that would flip the decision, which is actionable for the applicant.

questions.q: A partial dependence plot (PDP) shows:
options: The average prediction as one feature is varied while the others keep their real values
questions.explain: Set every applicant’s credit score to 550, 650, … and average the predictions each time.

questions.q: Why save the whole fitted pipeline (scaler + encoder + model) rather than only the model?
options: So production data is transformed exactly as in training, avoiding training–serving skew
The model cannot be saved alone
questions.explain: Unit 3’s get_dummies bug was exactly this kind of skew.

questions.q: Scoring every customer’s churn risk once a night and sending a call list to the retention team is:
questions.explain: Results are needed hours later, not within milliseconds.

questions.q: Checking every card transaction for fraud as it happens is best served by:
options: Re-training the model for every transaction
questions.explain: Fraud must be stopped before the payment completes.

questions.q: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") helps in production because:
options: A category never seen in training (e.g. “Freelancer”) does not crash the model
questions.explain: Unseen categories are encoded as all zeros instead of raising an error.

questions.q: In a real-time scoring API, the model should be loaded:
options: From the training notebook each time
questions.explain: Loading on every request would add large, avoidable latency.

questions.q: Which of these should a real-time scoring API do BEFORE predicting?
options: Validate that all required input fields are present and valid
questions.explain: Our API returns a clear 400 error listing missing fields instead of crashing.

questions.q: A feature store mainly helps by:
options: Computing features the same way for training and for live predictions
questions.explain: Consistent features prevent training–serving skew.

questions.q: Lowest PSI bin: expected share 0.099, actual 0.248. Its PSI term (A − E) × ln(A / E) is about:
A PSI of 0.339 on credit score means:
options: Significant drift: investigate and probably retrain
Only a minor change to watch
questions.explain: Rule of thumb: < 0.10 stable, 0.10–0.25 watch, > 0.25 significant.

questions.q: After an interest-rate rise, applicants with the same details default more often than before. This is:
questions.explain: The input → outcome relationship has changed; data drift is a change in the inputs themselves.

questions.q: Running a new model on live requests while it makes no real decisions, to compare it with the current one, is called:
questions.explain: It lets you check the challenger safely before replacing the champion.

questions.q: For diabetes screening, the clinic chose a threshold of 0.1 (recall 0.86, 289 of 450 referred) instead of 0.5 (recall 0.26). Why?
options: Missing a diabetic patient is far more costly than an extra blood test
A lower threshold always gives higher accuracy
questions.explain: In screening, recall comes first; the lab test then confirms.

questions.q: Why is logistic regression a common choice for credit scoring even when other models may be slightly more accurate?
options: Its coefficients give clear reason codes that lenders and regulators need
It is required by every bank’s software
questions.explain: India’s RBI Fair Practices Code asks lenders to tell applicants the main reasons for rejecting a loan.

questions.q: Applicant LN71318 has P(default) = 0.413 and the approval threshold is 0.25. The decision is:
options: Refer to a credit officer (not approved automatically)
questions.explain: 0.413 ≥ 0.25. Good practice routes such cases to a human rather than an automatic final no.

questions.q: Arrange the K-means algorithm steps in order.
options: Choose k and place starting centroids
Assign each point to its nearest centroid
Move each centroid to the mean of its points
questions.explain: Assign and update alternate until nothing changes.

questions.q: Customers at (1, 1), (1.5, 2) and (3, 4) form one cluster. Its updated centroid is:
Why must features be scaled before K-means on SwiftTel customers?
options: K-means uses distances, so monthly charge in rupees would otherwise dominate
Scaling reduces the number of clusters
questions.explain: Unscaled, the cluster structure would be driven almost only by price.

questions.q: Running K-means twice with k = 4 gave inertias 387.8 and 404.3. The best explanation is:
options: K-means can stop in a local minimum that depends on the starting centroids; run it several times and keep the best
Inertia is random noise and means nothing
questions.explain: That is why scikit-learn uses n_init = 10.

questions.q: Rural approval is 53.4% and urban approval 74.8%. The disparate impact ratio is about:
questions.explain: 0.534 / 0.748 = 0.714, below the common four-fifths (0.8) benchmark.

questions.q: The credit model never uses region, yet rural applicants are approved less often. The most likely cause here is:
options: A proxy: thin credit files make rural credit scores understate repayment ability
The model secretly reads the region column
Random noise in the test set
questions.explain: Actual default rates are similar (24.2% vs 23.1%); the score carries the disadvantage in.

questions.q: “Among applicants who would repay, approval rates should be similar across groups.” This fairness idea is:
questions.explain: Here it is violated: 83.6% urban vs 62.0% rural among good payers.

questions.q: Select ALL principles in India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 as described in this unit.
options: Processing personal data with consent for a specified purpose
Collecting only the data that is needed
Letting people access and correct their data
Selling data freely once it is collected
questions.explain: Consent, purpose limitation, data minimisation and individual rights are core ideas; free resale is not allowed.

questions.q: A lender declines a group, so that group never builds a repayment history, which makes the model decline them again. This is:
questions.explain: Monitoring outcomes and human review help break such loops.

questions.q: In an AI system, which task suits a generative AI model (LLM) alongside a credit-scoring model?
options: Writing a clear explanation letter to the applicant from the model’s reason codes
Replacing the need for any data
questions.explain: The predictive model decides; the LLM helps communicate (still with human oversight).

questions.q: AutoML tools such as IBM’s AutoAI mainly:
options: Automate preprocessing, model selection and hyperparameter tuning
Remove the need to define the business problem
questions.explain: People still frame the problem, check data quality and judge fairness.
